questions.text: In a region, electric potential varies as $V = 10 - 50x$ ($V$ in volts, $x$ in metres). The electric field in the region is:

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A conducting wire connects two charged metallic spheres A and B of radii $r_1$ and $r_2$ kept very far apart compared to their radii. The ratio of electric fields $(E_A/E_B)$ at their surfaces is:
questions.solution: Connected spheres reach equal potential $V = \frac{kq_1}{r_1} = \frac{kq_2}{r_2}$. Surface field $E = \frac{kq}{r^2} = \frac{V}{r}$, so $\frac{E_A}{E_B} = \frac{r_2}{r_1}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A long straight wire of circular cross-section (radius $a$) carries a steady current $I$ uniformly distributed across its cross-section. The magnetic field magnitude at distance $a/2$ from the axis is:
questions.solution: For $r < a$, $B = \frac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi a^2}$. At $r = a/2$, $B = \frac{\mu_0 I (a/2)}{2\pi a^2} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi a}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An electromagnetic wave passes from vacuum into a dielectric medium with relative permittivity $\varepsilon_r = 3/2$ and relative permeability $\mu_r = 8/3$. Then its:

options.text: wavelength is doubled and frequency remains unchanged
wavelength is doubled and frequency is halved
wavelength is halved and frequency remains unchanged
both wavelength and frequency remain unchanged

questions.solution: $n = \sqrt{\varepsilon_r \mu_r} = \sqrt{(3/2)(8/3)} = 2$. Frequency $\nu$ stays unchanged; $\lambda' = \lambda/n = \lambda/2$ (halved).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In a series LCR circuit, the voltage across the resistor, capacitor, and inductor is $10\text{ V}$ each. If the capacitor is short-circuited, the new voltage across the inductor will be:
questions.solution: Initially $V_L = V_C = 10\text{ V}$ and $V_R = 10\text{ V}$, so $V_{\text{source}} = 10\text{ V}$ and $X_L = X_C = R$. Shorting $C$ gives $Z' = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2} = \sqrt{2}R$. Thus $I' = \frac{V}{\sqrt{2}R}$ and $V_L' = I' X_L = \frac{10}{\sqrt{2}} = 5\sqrt{2}\text{ V}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A concave lens of focal length $10\text{ cm}$ is cut vertically into two identical plano-concave lenses. The focal length of each lens will be:
questions.solution: $\frac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left(-\frac{1}{R} - \frac{1}{R}\right) = -\frac{2(\mu-1)}{R} \Rightarrow \frac{(\mu-1)}{R} = \frac{1}{2|f|} = \frac{1}{20}$. For each plano-concave lens, $\frac{1}{|f'|} = \frac{\mu-1}{R} = \frac{1}{20} \Rightarrow f' = -20\text{ cm}$ (magnitude $20\text{ cm}$).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The 'distance of closest approach' of an $\alpha$-particle is $d$ when moving head-on with velocity $v$ towards a target nucleus. If its velocity is halved, the new distance of closest approach is:
questions.solution: $d = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{2Ze^2}{\frac{1}{2}mv^2} \propto \frac{1}{v^2}$. Halving $v$ makes $d' = 4d$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A straight long wire along the $y$-axis carries a current of $1\text{ A}$ along the $-y$ direction. The magnetic field at point $(50\text{ cm}, 0, 0)$ points along:
questions.solution: Using $\vec{B} \propto d\vec{l} \times \vec{r}$ with $d\vec{l}$ along $-\hat{j}$ and $\vec{r}$ along $+\hat{i}$: $(-\hat{j}) \times (+\hat{i}) = +\hat{k}$ ($+z$-axis).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A galvanometer of resistance $27\ \Omega$ is converted into an ammeter of range $0\text{--}10\text{ mA}$ using a $3\ \Omega$ shunt. The galvanometer shows full-scale deflection for a current of about:
questions.solution: $I_g = I \frac{S}{G + S} = 10\text{ mA} \times \frac{3}{27 + 3} = 1\text{ mA}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom, for large values of $n$, the distance between consecutive orbits is proportional to:
questions.solution: $r_n \propto n^2$. Gap between consecutive orbits is $r_{n+1} - r_n \propto (n+1)^2 - n^2 = 2n + 1 \propto n$ for large $n$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In an unbiased p-n junction at equilibrium, which statement is true?

options.text: Diffusion current is zero but drift current exists
Diffusion current exists but drift current is zero
Diffusion and drift currents are equal and opposite

questions.solution: At equilibrium in an unbiased p-n junction, diffusion current and drift current are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, making net current zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** All atoms have a net magnetic moment.

**Reason (R):** A current loop does not always behave as a magnetic dipole.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both A and R are false: diamagnetic atoms (paired electrons) have zero net magnetic moment, and any planar current loop behaves as a magnetic dipole of moment $\vec{m} = NIA$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its constituent nucleons.

**Reason (R):** Energy is absorbed when nucleons are bound together to form a nucleus.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: A is true (mass defect $\Delta m > 0$), but R is false because binding energy is released (not absorbed) when nucleons bind to form a nucleus.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** In Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom, energy levels are discrete and quantised.

**Reason (R):** The electrostatic force on the electron provides the necessary centripetal force to revolve around the nucleus.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain quantisation—quantisation comes from Bohr's angular momentum condition $L = nh/(2\pi)$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** Two electric heaters of power $P_1$ and $P_2$ ($P_2 > P_1$) are joined in series across a DC source of voltage $V$. The power consumed by the combination is less than that consumed by $P_1$ alone across the same source.

**Reason (R):** The power consumed by an electric device across a DC source of voltage $V$ is proportional to its resistance.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: In series, $R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 + R_2 > R_1$, so $P_{\text{series}} = V^2/R_{\text{eq}} < V^2/R_1 = P_1$ (A is true). For fixed $V$, $P = V^2/R$ is inversely (not directly) proportional to $R$ (R is false).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Two small identical metallic balls with charges $q$ and $-2q$ are separated by distance $r$ (initial force $F$). They are brought in contact and then separated to distance $r/2$. They will now:
questions.solution: Initial magnitude $|F| = \frac{k(2q^2)}{r^2}$. After contact, each gets $\frac{q - 2q}{2} = -\frac{q}{2}$. At distance $r/2$, they repel with $|F'| = \frac{k(q/2)^2}{(r/2)^2} = \frac{kq^2}{r^2} = \frac{F}{2}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Two wires of the same length and cross-sectional area, made of materials with resistivities $\rho_1$ and $\rho_2$, are connected in series. The equivalent resistivity of the combination is:
questions.solution: $R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 + R_2 \Rightarrow \rho_{\text{eq}} \frac{2L}{A} = \frac{\rho_1 L}{A} + \frac{\rho_2 L}{A} \Rightarrow \rho_{\text{eq}} = \frac{\rho_1 + \rho_2}{2}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A wire is gradually stretched to increase its length by $100\%$. The percentage increase in its resistance is:
questions.solution: Length increases by $100\% \Rightarrow l' = 2l$. Volume constant $\Rightarrow R' = 4R$. Percentage increase $= \frac{4R - R}{R} \times 100\% = 300\%$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A magnet held vertically with its North pole down is dropped along the axis of a closed vertical solenoid on a table. An observer looking down from the top sees:

options.text: the magnet falling with constant velocity

questions.solution: By Lenz's law, the top face of the solenoid develops a North pole to oppose the approaching North pole. Looking from above, North polarity corresponds to anticlockwise—wait: let's re-check Lenz's law carefully! North pole approaches from top $\Rightarrow$ flux downward increases $\Rightarrow$ induced field opposes downward flux, i.e., points UPWARD from top face. Right-hand thumb upward $\Rightarrow$ fingers curl ANTICLOCKWISE when viewed from top! Let's verify: thumb up = anticlockwise from top. Good catch checking direction!

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The magnetic field of a plane EM wave in glass ($n = 1.5$) is $B_y = (2 \times 10^{-7}\text{ T})\sin(\alpha x + 1.5 \times 10^{11} t)$ ($x$ in m, $t$ in s). The value of $\alpha$ is:
questions.solution: Speed in glass $v = c/n = (3 \times 10^8)/1.5 = 2 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$. $\alpha = k = \frac{\omega}{v} = \frac{1.5 \times 10^{11}}{2 \times 10^8} = 7.5 \times 10^2\text{ m}^{-1}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The ratio of the amplitude of the electric field to the amplitude of the magnetic field for an EM wave propagating in glass ($n = 1.5$) is:
questions.solution: $\frac{E_0}{B_0} = v = \frac{c}{n} = \frac{3 \times 10^8}{1.5} = 2 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An AC voltage is given by $v = 14\sin(314t)\text{ V}$. Its average value and effective (rms) value over a full cycle are respectively:
questions.solution: Average over a full cycle is $0\text{ V}$; $V_{\text{rms}} = \frac{14}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 10\text{ V}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A thin plano-convex lens and a thin equi-concave lens (both glass of index $\mu$, curvature radius $R$) are placed coaxially in contact. The focal length of the combination is:
questions.solution: $\frac{1}{f_1} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R} - \frac{1}{\infty}\right) = \frac{\mu-1}{R}$. $\frac{1}{f_2} = (\mu - 1)\left(-\frac{1}{R} - \frac{1}{R}\right) = -\frac{2(\mu-1)}{R}$. $\frac{1}{f_{\text{eq}}} = -\frac{\mu-1}{R} \Rightarrow f_{\text{eq}} = -\frac{R}{\mu-1}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A proton and an $\alpha$-particle have equal momentum. The ratio of their kinetic energies $(E_p/E_\alpha)$ and de Broglie wavelengths $(\lambda_p/\lambda_\alpha)$ respectively are:
questions.solution: Equal $p$: $\lambda = h/p \Rightarrow \lambda_p/\lambda_\alpha = 1$. $K = p^2/(2m) \Rightarrow E_p/E_\alpha = m_\alpha / m_p = 4m_p / m_p = 4$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The kinetic energy of a charged particle is increased to four times its initial value. Its de Broglie wavelength will:
questions.solution: $\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}} \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{K}}$. If $K' = 4K$, $\lambda' = \lambda/2$, which is a $50\%$ decrease.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In Bohr's H-atom model, an electron jumps from $n = 5 \to 1$ emitting wavelength $\lambda$. If it jumps from $n = 5 \to 2$, the emitted wavelength will be:
questions.solution: $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(1 - \frac{1}{25}\right) = \frac{24R}{25}$. $\frac{1}{\lambda'} = R\left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{25}\right) = \frac{21R}{100} = \frac{7R}{100/3}$. Ratio $\frac{\lambda'}{\lambda} = \frac{24}{25} \times \frac{100}{21} = \frac{24}{7}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The process named 'minority carrier injection' in a p-n junction diode occurs during:
questions.solution: In forward bias, majority carriers cross the junction and become minority carriers on the other side—called minority carrier injection.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** The cylindrical soft iron core in a moving coil galvanometer only makes the magnetic field radial and does not affect the strength of the magnetic field.

**Reason (R):** In a moving coil galvanometer, the plane of the coil is always perpendicular to the magnetic field.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both are false: soft iron core both makes the field radial and increases its strength; in a radial field, the coil's plane is parallel (not perpendicular) to $\vec{B}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** When a ferromagnetic substance is heated to high temperature, it becomes paramagnetic in nature.

**Reason (R):** The disappearance of magnetisation of a ferromagnet is abrupt and not gradual.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: A is true above Curie temperature; R is false because magnetisation decreases gradually with temperature.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** Nuclear forces are always attractive.

**Reason (R):** The nuclear force between protons and neutrons in a nucleus is a weak force.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both are false: nuclear forces are repulsive at very short distances ($< 0.8\text{ fm}$) and are strong nuclear forces, not weak.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** Photoelectric effect is a spontaneous (instantaneous) phenomenon.

**Reason (R):** According to the wave picture of radiation, an electron would take hours/days to absorb sufficient energy to overcome the work function and escape a metal surface.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both statements are true, but R explains why wave theory fails—it does not explain why the effect is instantaneous.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A body acquires a charge of $+8.0 \times 10^{-12}\text{ C}$. The mass of the body:
questions.solution: Positive charge means electrons are removed: $n = \frac{8.0 \times 10^{-12}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 5 \times 10^7$. Mass decreases by $n m_e = 5 \times 10^7 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \approx 4.55 \times 10^{-23}\text{ kg}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A metal sheet is inserted between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor of capacitance $C$. If the sheet partly occupies the space between the plates, the capacitance:
questions.solution: Effective separation reduces from $d$ to $(d - t)$, so $C' = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d - t} > C$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A rectangular coil of area $A$ is kept in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ such that the plane of the coil makes an angle $\alpha$ with $\vec{B}$. The magnetic flux linked with the coil is:
questions.solution: Angle between area normal and $\vec{B}$ is $(90^\circ - \alpha)$, so $\Phi = BA\cos(90^\circ - \alpha) = BA\sin\alpha$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A piece of a diamagnetic material, free to move, is placed in a uniform magnetic field. It:
questions.solution: In a uniform magnetic field, there is no net translational force on a diamagnetic sample, so it does not move.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A vertically held bar magnet is dropped along the axis of a copper ring having a cut. The acceleration of the falling magnet is:
questions.solution: Because of the cut, the loop is open—no induced current flows, no opposing magnetic force acts, and acceleration equals $g$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An alternating current is given by $I = I_0 \cos(100\pi t)$. The least time the current takes to decrease from its maximum value to zero is:
questions.solution: $I = 0$ first when $\cos(100\pi t) = 0 \Rightarrow 100\pi t = \pi/2 \Rightarrow t = \frac{1}{200}\text{ s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A capacitor and an inductor are connected in series across a variable-frequency AC source. As frequency is increased continuously, the nature of the circuit before and after resonance is:
questions.solution: Below resonance ($f < f_0$), $X_C > X_L$ (capacitive); above resonance ($f > f_0$), $X_L > X_C$ (inductive).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Two coherent waves, each of intensity $I_0$, produce an interference pattern on a screen. The average intensity of light on the screen is:
questions.solution: $I = 4I_0\cos^2(\phi/2)$. Average of $\cos^2(\phi/2)$ is $1/2$, so $I_{\text{avg}} = 4I_0 (1/2) = 2I_0$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A beam of red light and a beam of blue light have equal intensities. Which statement is true?

options.text: The blue beam has more photons than the red beam
The red beam has more photons than the blue beam
Wavelength of red light is less than that of blue light
Blue light has less energy per photon than red light

questions.solution: Red has longer wavelength $\Rightarrow$ lower photon energy $h c/\lambda$. For equal intensity $I = n h\nu$, more photons per second are needed in the red beam.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The work function of a material is $2.21\text{ eV}$. Which of the following cannot produce photoelectrons from it?
questions.solution: Red light has photon energy around $1.8\text{ eV} < 2.21\text{ eV}$, below the threshold work function.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Out of the following transitions in a hydrogen atom, which emits a photon of maximum wavelength?
questions.solution: Maximum wavelength corresponds to minimum energy gap $\Delta E = hc/\lambda$. Among the choices, $n = 4 \to 3$ has the smallest energy difference.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A germanium crystal is doped at room temperature with a minute quantity of boron. The charge carriers in the doped semiconductor will be:
questions.solution: Boron is trivalent (p-type), so holes are majority carriers and thermally generated electrons are minority carriers ('holes and few electrons').

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** A charged particle moves with velocity $\vec{v}$ in the $x$-$y$ plane making an angle $\theta$ ($0 < \theta < \pi/2$) with the $x$-axis. If a uniform magnetic field is applied along the $y$-axis, the particle moves in a helical path with its axis parallel to the $x$-axis.

**Reason (R):** The magnetic force on a moving charged particle is directed along its velocity.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both are false: velocity component along $y$ is parallel to $\vec{B}$ (helical axis is parallel to $y$-axis, not $x$), and magnetic force $q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$ is perpendicular to $\vec{v}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** A hole is an apparent free particle with an effective positive electronic charge.

**Reason (R):** A hole is not necessarily a vacancy left behind by an electron in the valence band.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: A is true, while R is false because a hole in a semiconductor is by definition an absence/vacancy of an electron in the valence band.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** The binding energy per nucleon is practically constant for mass numbers in the range $30 < A < 170$.

**Reason (R):** Nuclear forces between nucleons in the range $30 < A < 170$ are not short-range.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: A is true, but R is false because the constancy (saturation) is due to the short-range nature of nuclear forces.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** An n-type semiconductor is not negatively charged.

**Reason (R):** A neutral pentavalent impurity atom doped in a neutral intrinsic semiconductor donates its fifth unpaired electron to the crystal lattice and becomes a positive donor ion.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both A and R are true and R explains why the doped crystal remains electrically neutral overall.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A parallel plate capacitor is charged by a battery, and the battery is then disconnected. If a dielectric slab of constant $K$ is now fully inserted between the plates, the electrostatic energy stored in the capacitor:
questions.solution: Charge $Q$ is constant and $C' = KC$. Stored energy $U' = \frac{Q^2}{2C'} = \frac{Q^2}{2KC} = \frac{U}{K}$ (decreases by factor $K$).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A steady current flows through a metallic conductor of non-uniform cross-section. Which of the following quantities remains constant along the conductor?
questions.solution: In steady state with no charge accumulation, electric current $I$ is constant across every cross-section; $J$, $v_d$, and $E$ vary inversely with area $A$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: If the number of turns in a moving coil galvanometer is doubled (keeping the wire thickness, coil area, $B$, and spring constant the same), then its current sensitivity and voltage sensitivity respectively:
questions.solution: Current sensitivity $I_s = \frac{NBA}{k}$ doubles when $N \to 2N$. For identical wire thickness/length per turn, $R$ also doubles, so voltage sensitivity $V_s = \frac{I_s}{R}$ remains unchanged.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes the magnetic susceptibility ($\chi$) of a diamagnetic substance as temperature increases?

options.text: Negative and remains independent of temperature

questions.solution: Diamagnetic susceptibility is small, negative, and independent of temperature.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A closely wound long solenoid of self-inductance $L$ is cut into two identical smaller solenoids. The self-inductance of each smaller solenoid is:
questions.solution: For a solenoid, $L = \mu_0 n^2 A l$. Turns per unit length $n$ and area $A$ stay same; length halves ($l' = l/2$), so $L' = L/2$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In a series LCR circuit at resonance, if the frequency of the AC source is doubled (keeping peak voltage constant), the current in the circuit:
questions.solution: Above resonance ($f > f_0$), $X_L > X_C$, impedance $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$ increases, so current decreases and voltage leads current (current lags behind voltage).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In a plane electromagnetic wave propagating in vacuum, the ratio of average electric energy density ($u_E$) to average magnetic energy density ($u_B$) is:
questions.solution: In an EM wave, electric and magnetic fields carry equal average energy densities: $u_E = u_B = \frac{1}{4}\varepsilon_0 E_0^2 = \frac{B_0^2}{4\mu_0}$, so $u_E/u_B = 1$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Which electromagnetic waves are produced by rapid deceleration of high-speed electrons hitting a heavy metal target, and what is their approximate wavelength range?
questions.solution: X-rays are produced by deceleration of fast electrons in heavy metal targets and span roughly $1\text{ nm}$ to $10^{-3}\text{ nm}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A double-convex lens made of glass ($n = 1.5$) is completely immersed in carbon disulphide ($n = 1.65$). The lens will now behave as a:

options.text: converging lens of smaller focal length
converging lens of larger focal length

questions.solution: Since $n_{\text{medium}} = 1.65 > n_{\text{lens}} = 1.5$, $(n_2/n_1 - 1)$ becomes negative, flipping a double-convex lens into a diverging lens.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In a single-slit diffraction experiment, if the slit width $a$ is halved while keeping wavelength $\lambda$ and screen distance $D$ constant, the angular width of the central maximum:
questions.solution: Angular half-width is $\theta = \lambda/a$, so full angular width $2\theta = 2\lambda/a$ doubles when $a$ is halved.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The stopping potential ($V_0$) versus frequency ($\nu$) graphs for two different metals A and B are plotted on the same axes. The two straight lines are always:

options.text: having different slopes proportional to their work functions

questions.solution: $eV_0 = h\nu - \phi_0 \Rightarrow V_0 = \left(\frac{h}{e}\right)\nu - \frac{\phi_0}{e}$. All metals have the same slope $h/e$, so the lines are parallel.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A full-wave rectifier is fed with an AC input of frequency $50\text{ Hz}$. The fundamental frequency of the pulsating DC output across the load resistor is:
questions.solution: A full-wave rectifier inverts negative half-cycles, doubling output ripple frequency to $2f = 100\text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** The magnetic susceptibility of a diamagnetic substance is independent of temperature.

**Reason (R):** Diamagnetism is an induced effect caused by the modification of orbital motion of electrons opposing the applied magnetic field, not by thermal alignment of permanent dipoles.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains why thermal agitation does not alter diamagnetic susceptibility.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** During charging of a parallel plate capacitor, a magnetic field exists in the region between the plates even though no conduction current flows through the gap.

**Reason (R):** A time-varying electric flux between the plates gives rise to a displacement current that acts as a source of magnetic field.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both A and R are true and Maxwell's displacement current $i_d = \varepsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$ directly explains the magnetic field between the plates.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** At absolute zero ($0\text{ K}$), an intrinsic semiconductor behaves as a perfect insulator.

**Reason (R):** At $0\text{ K}$, all covalent bonds in a pure semiconductor are intact and no free electrons are available in the conduction band.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both A and R are true and R explains why conduction does not occur at $0\text{ K}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** The nuclear density is almost constant and independent of mass number $A$ for all nuclei.

**Reason (R):** The radius of a nucleus is directly proportional to its mass number $A$.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: A is true, but R is false because nuclear radius scales as $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$ (cube root, not direct proportion).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** No work is done in moving a test charge between any two points on the surface of a charged metallic conductor in electrostatic equilibrium.

**Reason (R):** Every point on the surface of a charged conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is at the same electric potential.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both are true; $\Delta V = 0 \Rightarrow W = q\Delta V = 0$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** When a dielectric slab is inserted between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor while it remains connected to a battery, the electric field between the plates decreases.

**Reason (R):** Inserting a dielectric slab into a capacitor always reduces the potential difference across its plates.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both are false when connected to a battery: $V$ stays fixed by the battery, and $E = V/d$ also remains unchanged.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** For a metallic conductor, resistivity increases with an increase in temperature.

**Reason (R):** With an increase in temperature, the number density of free electrons ($n$) in a metal decreases sharply.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: A is true (relaxation time $\tau$ decreases), but R is false because $n$ in a metal stays nearly constant.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** The terminal potential difference across a cell can never exceed its emf.

**Reason (R):** The terminal potential difference of a cell is always given by $V = E - Ir$, where $I$ is the current passing through it.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both are false: when a cell is being charged, $V = E + Ir > E$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** A uniform magnetic field does zero work on a moving charged particle.

**Reason (R):** The radius of the circular path of a charged particle entering perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field is directly proportional to its linear momentum.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both are true ($\vec{F}_B \perp \vec{v}$ so work is zero, and $r = p/(qB)$), but R does not explain why work is zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** When a diamagnetic material is placed in an external magnetic field, the magnetic field lines are expelled from it.

**Reason (R):** The relative magnetic permeability ($\mu_r$) of a diamagnetic material is slightly greater than $1$.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: A is true, but R is false because for diamagnetic materials $\mu_r < 1$ (slightly less than $1$).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** Magnetic field lines can intersect each other inside a bar magnet.

**Reason (R):** Inside a bar magnet, magnetic field lines are directed from the North pole to the South pole.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both are false: magnetic field lines never intersect, and inside a magnet they run from South to North.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** The magnetisation of a paramagnetic sample decreases when its temperature is increased (for the same magnetising field).

**Reason (R):** Paramagnetic materials tend to move from weaker to stronger regions of a non-uniform magnetic field.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both are true (Curie's law and paramagnetic attraction), but R does not explain temperature dependence of magnetisation.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** If a copper ring with a small cut in it is moved into a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its plane, an emf is induced across the cut ends.

**Reason (R):** Induced emf depends on the rate of change of magnetic flux linked with the loop, regardless of whether the loop is closed or open.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both are true and R correctly explains why emf is induced even in an open/cut loop.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** A capacitor blocks steady direct current (DC) but allows alternating current (AC) to pass through.

**Reason (R):** Capacitive reactance is directly proportional to the frequency of the applied voltage.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: A is true, but R is false because $X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi f C}$ is inversely proportional to frequency.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** In a pure inductive AC circuit, the average power dissipated over a complete cycle is zero.

**Reason (R):** In a pure inductive AC circuit, the current leads the applied voltage by a phase angle of $\pi/2$.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: A is true ($P_{\text{avg}} = V_{\text{rms}} I_{\text{rms}} \cos 90^\circ = 0$), but R is false because current lags behind voltage by $\pi/2$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** During the charging of a parallel plate capacitor, the displacement current between the plates is equal in magnitude to the conduction current in the connecting wires.

**Reason (R):** Both conduction current and displacement current produce a magnetic field.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both are true, but R does not explain why their magnitudes are equal (charge conservation / continuity gives $i_d = i_c$).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** A charged particle moving with a constant velocity produces electromagnetic waves.

**Reason (R):** Infrared waves have a shorter wavelength than ultraviolet waves.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both are false: accelerated (not constant-velocity) charges produce EM waves, and IR has longer wavelength than UV.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** In an optical fibre, the refractive index of the core must be greater than the refractive index of the cladding.

**Reason (R):** Total internal reflection occurs only when light travels from an optically rarer medium to an optically denser medium.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: A is true, but R is false because TIR requires light to travel from optically denser to rarer medium.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** Two independent sodium lamps placed close to each other cannot produce a sustained interference pattern on a screen.

**Reason (R):** The phase difference between light waves emitted by two independent sources changes rapidly and randomly with time.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both are true and R explains why independent sources are incoherent and cannot sustain a stationary interference pattern.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** In a photoelectric experiment, increasing the intensity of incident light (above threshold frequency) increases the saturation photocurrent.

**Reason (R):** Increasing the intensity of incident light increases the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: A is true, but R is false because maximum kinetic energy depends on frequency, not intensity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** The total energy of an electron in a bound orbit of a hydrogen atom is negative.

**Reason (R):** As the electron moves to a higher orbit ($n$ increases), its kinetic energy decreases while its potential energy increases.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both are true, but R describes how $K$ and $U$ change with $n$, not why total energy $E = -\frac{e^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$ is negative (bound state).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** Nuclear fusion reactions require extremely high temperatures (of the order of $10^7\text{ K}$) to take place.

**Reason (R):** Positively charged light nuclei require very high kinetic energy to overcome the strong electrostatic Coulomb repulsion between them.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both are true and R gives the physical reason for needing high thermal kinetic energy.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** The electrical conductivity of a pure semiconductor increases with an increase in temperature.

**Reason (R):** With an increase in temperature, the number of thermally generated electron-hole pairs increases exponentially, outweighing the decrease in relaxation time.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both are true and R is the exact explanation for rising conductivity in intrinsic semiconductors.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
**Assertion (A):** When a p-n junction diode is reverse biased, both the width of the depletion region and the effective barrier height increase.

**Reason (R):** Under reverse bias, the small reverse saturation current is due to the drift of minority charge carriers across the junction.

options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

questions.solution: Both are true statements, but R explains the reverse current rather than the widening of the depletion layer / increased barrier height.

flipcards.subject: Physics
flipcards.title: Electric Field Inside Solid Sphere
flipcards.prompt: Electric field at distance r ≤ R from center of a uniformly charged non-conducting solid sphere
flipcards.vars: ρ = volume charge density (C/m³), Q = total charge, R = radius, r = distance from center
flipcards.tip: E ∝ r inside (zero at center) and peaks at surface r = R

flipcards.subject: Physics
flipcards.title: Electric Field Inside Spherical Cavity
flipcards.prompt: Uniform electric field inside a spherical cavity (center O₂) inside a solid sphere (center O₁)
flipcards.vars: ρ = volume charge density, O₁O₂ = vector from sphere center to cavity center
flipcards.tip: Field is uniform and completely independent of cavity radius; denominator is 2ε₀ for a cylinder

flipcards.subject: Physics
flipcards.title: Axial Electric Field of Charged Ring
flipcards.prompt: Electric field on the axis of a uniformly charged ring of radius R at axial distance x
flipcards.vars: Q = total ring charge, R = ring radius, x = axial distance, k = 1/(4πε₀)
flipcards.tip: Maximum at x = ±R/√2; behaves as point charge kQ/x² when x ≫ R

flipcards.subject: Physics
flipcards.title: Work Done by Battery on Inserting Dielectric
flipcards.prompt: Work done by constant-voltage battery V when dielectric K fills capacitor C
flipcards.vars: K = dielectric constant, C = initial air capacitance, V = battery voltage
flipcards.tip: Half goes to ΔU = ½(K−1)CV², half is mechanical work/heat

flipcards.subject: Physics
flipcards.title: Drift Velocity & Microscopic Resistance
flipcards.prompt: Express drift velocity v_d and resistance R in terms of relaxation time τ
flipcards.latex: v_d = \frac{e E \tau}{m} \quad | \quad R = \frac{m l}{n e^2 \tau A}
flipcards.vars: n = free electron density, τ = relaxation time, m = electron mass, A = cross-section
flipcards.tip: As temperature rises, τ drops so metallic resistivity ρ = m/(ne²τ) increases

flipcards.subject: Physics
flipcards.title: Motional EMF (General Vector Form)
flipcards.prompt: Motional EMF induced across a straight conductor of length vector L moving at velocity v in field B
flipcards.vars: v = velocity vector, B = magnetic field vector, L = conductor length vector
flipcards.tip: Zero if any two of v, B, L are parallel or all three are coplanar

flipcards.subject: Physics
flipcards.title: RLC Series Resonance & Quality Factor
flipcards.prompt: Resonant angular frequency ω₀ and quality factor Q of a series RLC circuit
flipcards.vars: L = inductance (H), C = capacitance (F), R = resistance (Ω)
flipcards.tip: At resonance, X_L = X_C, impedance Z = R (minimum), and power factor cos φ = 1

flipcards.subject: Physics
flipcards.title: de Broglie Wavelength of Accelerated Electron
flipcards.prompt: Shortcut wavelength λ (in Å) for an electron accelerated through potential V (in volts)
flipcards.vars: V = accelerating potential (Volts), h = Planck constant
flipcards.tip: For 100 V, λ ≈ 1.227 Å — memorize 12.27/√V for fast JEE calculations

flipcards.subject: Chemistry
flipcards.title: LiAlH4 + Ethanamide
flipcards.prompt: Predict the major product:
flipcards.vars: Converts amide C=O to CH₂ with same carbon count
flipcards.tip: Trap: gives an AMINE, not an alcohol! Hofmann (Br₂/KOH) drops 1 carbon

flipcards.subject: Chemistry
flipcards.title: DIBAL-H + Ethyl Propanoate
flipcards.prompt: Predict the major product:
flipcards.vars: Bulky hydride donor at low temp stops at aldehyde
flipcards.tip: Also reduces nitriles (R-CN) to aldehydes at -78 °C

flipcards.subject: Chemistry
flipcards.title: SOCl2 vs SOCl2 + Pyridine
flipcards.prompt: Compare stereochemistry on (R)-Butan-2-ol:
flipcards.vars: Darzen's halogenation; SO₂↑ and HCl↑ escape as gases
flipcards.tip: Adding pyridine flips Retention → Inversion!

flipcards.subject: Chemistry
flipcards.title: Na / liq. NH3 + Propyne (Terminal Alkyne)
flipcards.prompt: Predict the major product:
flipcards.vars: Acid-base reaction forming sodium propynide
flipcards.tip: Trap: internal alkynes give trans-alkene, but terminal alkynes form acetylide salt!

flipcards.subject: Chemistry
flipcards.title: First-Order Rate Law & Half-Life
flipcards.prompt: Integrated rate constant k and half-life t₁/₂ for a first-order reaction
flipcards.vars: [A]₀ = initial concentration, [A]_t = concentration at time t
flipcards.tip: t₁/₂ is completely independent of initial concentration; t_99.9% ≈ 10 × t₁/₂

flipcards.subject: Chemistry
flipcards.title: Nernst Equation at 298 K
flipcards.prompt: Cell potential E_cell at 298 K in terms of standard potential E°_cell and reaction quotient Q
flipcards.vars: n = moles of electrons transferred, Q = reaction quotient
flipcards.tip: At equilibrium E_cell = 0, so E°_cell = (0.0591/n) log K_c

flipcards.subject: Chemistry
flipcards.title: Gibbs Free Energy & Equilibrium Constant
flipcards.prompt: Relate ΔG, ΔG°, and equilibrium constant K
flipcards.latex: \Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q \quad | \quad \Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K = -nFE^\circ_{\text{cell}}
flipcards.vars: R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), T = temperature (K), F = 96500 C/mol
flipcards.tip: For spontaneity at constant T, P: ΔG < 0 (not necessarily ΔG° < 0)

flipcards.subject: Chemistry
flipcards.title: Colligative Properties with van't Hoff Factor
flipcards.prompt: Boiling point elevation, freezing point depression, and osmotic pressure
flipcards.latex: \Delta T_b = i K_b m \quad | \quad \Delta T_f = i K_f m \quad | \quad \Pi = i C R T
flipcards.vars: i = 1 + (n−1)α for dissociation; m = molality, C = molarity
flipcards.tip: Remember to multiply by van't Hoff factor i for electrolytes like Na₂SO₄ (i = 3)!

flipcards.subject: Mathematics
flipcards.title: King's Property of Definite Integrals
flipcards.prompt: Standard symmetry substitution for integrating f(x) from a to b
flipcards.vars: Valid for any integrable function f on [a, b]
flipcards.tip: Add the original and transformed integrals to cancel complex denominators

flipcards.subject: Mathematics
flipcards.title: Leibniz Rule (Differentiation Under Integral)
flipcards.prompt: Derivative of a definite integral with variable limits g(x) and h(x)
flipcards.vars: f continuous, g and h differentiable
flipcards.tip: Frequently paired with L'Hôpital's Rule in JEE Main limit problems

flipcards.subject: Mathematics
flipcards.title: Linear Differential Equation Solution
flipcards.prompt: Integrating factor (I.F.) and general solution for dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x)
flipcards.vars: P(x), Q(x) are functions of x only
flipcards.tip: Always normalize the coefficient of dy/dx to 1 before finding P(x)!

flipcards.subject: Mathematics
flipcards.title: Shortest Distance Between Skew Lines
flipcards.prompt: Shortest distance d between lines r = a₁ + λb₁ and r = a₂ + μb₂
flipcards.vars: a₁, a₂ = position vectors on lines; b₁, b₂ = direction vectors
flipcards.tip: If b₁ × b₂ = 0 (parallel lines), use d = |(a₂ − a₁) × b| / |b| instead

flipcards.subject: Mathematics
flipcards.title: Vector Triple Product (BAC-CAB Rule)
flipcards.prompt: Expand a × (b × c) as a linear combination of b and c
flipcards.vars: Lies in the plane of b and c, perpendicular to a
flipcards.tip: Warning: Vector triple product is NOT associative: a×(b×c) ≠ (a×b)×c

flipcards.subject: Mathematics
flipcards.title: Properties of Adjoint Matrix
flipcards.prompt: Determinant of adj(A) and adj(adj(A)) for an n × n non-singular matrix A
flipcards.vars: n = order of square matrix A
flipcards.tip: Also remember: adj(kA) = k^(n−1) adj(A) and |kA| = k^n |A|

flipcards.subject: Mathematics
flipcards.title: Bayes' Theorem
flipcards.prompt: Posterior probability P(E_i | A) given mutually exclusive events E₁, ..., E_n
flipcards.vars: E_i form a partition of sample space S; P(A) > 0
flipcards.tip: Draw a quick probability tree to avoid swapping P(A|E) and P(E|A)

flipcards.subject: Mathematics
flipcards.title: Tangent to Ellipse & Hyperbola (Slope Form)
flipcards.prompt: Equation of tangent of slope m to standard ellipse and hyperbola
flipcards.latex: y = mx \pm \sqrt{a^2 m^2 + b^2} \quad | \quad y = mx \pm \sqrt{a^2 m^2 - b^2}
flipcards.vars: a, b = semi-axes; m = slope of tangent
flipcards.tip: For ellipse use +b²; for hyperbola use −b² (valid when a²m² > b²)
